client: I've been really stressed out lately because of my new job — I'm a project manager, and we missed a major deadline last week, and I just can't stop replaying everything in my head. I keep thinking about what I should have done differently, and honestly the guilt is eating me alive. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy weight right now — the stress of a new role, the pressure of that missed deadline, and your mind working overtime trying to find answers. That kind of relentless replaying can be exhausting, and the guilt you're describing makes a lot of sense given how much you clearly care about doing well. I'm glad you gave this a shot — can you tell me a little more about what the inner critic is saying when it replays those moments?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Mostly it's just this constant voice telling me I should have caught the bottleneck in the timeline earlier — like, I saw the warning signs and I didn't act fast enough, and now the whole team looks bad because of me. It also keeps saying things like "you're not cut out for this role" and "everyone can see you don't know what you're doing." It's hard to push back on those thoughts because honestly, part of me wonders if they're actually true.
therapist: Those thoughts — "you're not cut out for this" and "everyone can see you're failing" — are incredibly harsh, and I notice there's a real urgency in how you're describing all of this, like the weight of it feels very immediate and pressing right now. What I want to gently ask is: if a colleague came to you and said they'd missed a deadline in their first months in a new role, would you tell them they're not cut out for it — or would you see it differently for them than you do for yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean, no, obviously I wouldn't say that to a colleague — I'd probably tell them it happens and that they should figure out what went wrong and move on. But it feels different when it's me, because I'm the one who was supposed to be leading the team, so the responsibility lands harder. I get what you're doing with that question, but I'm not sure just recognizing the double standard actually makes the guilt go away.
therapist: You're absolutely right that insight alone doesn't dissolve guilt — and I appreciate you pushing back on that, because it's an important point. What strikes me is that even as you're explaining this clearly and logically, there's something in how you're speaking that sounds almost... small, like you're carrying something heavier than the words alone are letting on. I'm wondering — underneath the guilt about the deadline, is there a deeper fear at play, maybe something about what this mistake means about you and whether you belong in this role at all?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah, I think that's probably it — like, this job was a big step up for me, and some part of me has been waiting for people to figure out that I don't actually deserve it. The missed deadline felt like proof of that, like the thing I'd been dreading finally happened and now it's only a matter of time before everyone else sees it too. I don't even know how to explain that fear to my team or my manager without sounding like I'm falling apart.
therapist: What you're describing has a name — it's often called impostor syndrome, and it's remarkably common in people who've worked hard to earn a step up, which makes it no less painful but does mean you're not alone in this. I notice as you're sharing something so vulnerable, your voice sounds quite soft and measured — like you've been holding this fear very carefully, maybe for a long time. Can you tell me more about where that belief that you "don't deserve" this role comes from — is it something that's followed you before this job, or does it feel new?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, it's not new — I've felt this way in pretty much every job I've had, like I somehow slipped through the cracks and got further than I was supposed to. I grew up in a household where nothing I did was ever quite good enough, and I think that voice in my head kind of sounds like my dad, if I'm being honest. I'm not sure how much digging into all of that is going to help me get through next week's team meeting though.
therapist: That connection you just made — between your dad's voice and the critic in your head — is really significant, and it takes courage to name that. I notice you said it quite quickly, almost like you wanted to move past it, and then immediately redirected to next week's meeting — and I want to honor that you have real, practical things to prepare for. But I'm curious: do you think that inner voice telling you you're not good enough might be making next week's meeting feel even more daunting than it needs to be?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, probably — I keep imagining walking into that meeting and everyone just looking at me like I've already failed them, and I can't tell how much of that is realistic versus my brain just spiraling. But even if I accept that the voice is distorted or coming from old stuff with my dad, I still have to actually stand up in front of those people and explain what went wrong. I guess I'm just not sure how quieting that inner critic is supposed to translate into feeling more confident in the moment.
therapist: That's such an honest and important question — you're right that awareness isn't the same as confidence, and the gap between the two is exactly where the real work happens. What I'd gently offer is that the goal isn't to walk into that meeting feeling fearless, but to be able to notice the spiral starting — "there's my dad's voice again" — and choose how you respond to it rather than being swept along by it. What do you think it would feel like to walk in there not needing to prove you deserve the role, but just focused on what the team needs from you in that moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That actually sounds kind of relieving to imagine, but I'm not sure I know how to just switch off the need to prove myself — it feels pretty deeply wired in at this point. Like, even right now thinking about it, I can feel my chest tightening because part of me is convinced that if I stop trying to prove myself, I'll just fall apart completely. How do I even practice that shift before Thursday when the meeting is in two days?
therapist: That image of "falling apart" if you stop proving yourself is really worth holding onto, because it tells us something important — that part of you believes the constant striving is the only thing keeping you together, when in reality it might be part of what's exhausting you. For the next two days, one small practice could be to notice when that proving impulse kicks in and just pause for a breath, reminding yourself that your job Thursday isn't to be perfect but to be present and honest with your team. What would it look like to open that meeting by briefly acknowledging what happened and what you've learned — not as a confession, but as a leader taking ownership?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: I think I could probably do something like that — acknowledge the delay, explain what we're changing going forward — but my worry is that the moment I start talking, I'll either over-explain and sound defensive, or I'll under-explain and seem like I don't care. And then there's this other part of me that's afraid if I show any vulnerability in front of the team, they'll lose confidence in me completely, which feels like the worst possible outcome. I guess I'm just not sure there's a version of that conversation where I come out feeling okay about myself afterward.
therapist: The fear you're describing — that there's no version of this where you come out okay — sounds like your mind is foreclosing on possibilities before Thursday even arrives, which is worth noticing. What's striking is that you're imagining your team's confidence in you as something fragile that vulnerability would shatter, but research and experience consistently show that leaders who own mistakes clearly and calmly often gain trust rather than lose it. I want to ask — when you've seen someone else take accountability for something that went wrong, did it make you lose respect for them, or did it actually do the opposite?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: When you put it that way, yeah, I've actually respected people more when they owned their mistakes — there was a manager I had a few years ago who stood up in front of everyone and said "I got this wrong, here's what we're doing differently," and I remember thinking she was the most credible person in the room. But it's easier to see that clearly when it's someone else, because I don't have the same emotional stake in their outcome that I have in mine. I guess part of me is still worried that the rules work differently for me, like other people get to be human but I somehow don't.
therapist: What you just said — "other people get to be human but I somehow don't" — is one of the most important things you've shared today, and I think that belief is at the heart of so much of what you're carrying. I notice you arrived at that insight quickly, almost like the words came rushing out, and I want to make sure we don't move past it too fast — because that rule you've been living by, that you're held to a different and harsher standard than everyone else, sounds exhausting to carry. Where do you think you first learned that the normal allowances for being human didn't apply to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think I learned it pretty young — my dad had really high standards and when I made mistakes, the response was never "that's okay, you'll do better next time," it was more like disappointment or silence, which somehow felt worse than anger. So I think I just internalized that errors meant something was fundamentally wrong with me, not just that I'd done something wrong. It's strange to say all of this out loud because I've kind of known it on some level for a long time, but I've never really connected it to how I'm feeling about this job stuff until right now.
therapist: What you just connected is really profound — that silence from your dad didn't just hurt, it taught you that mistakes meant something was broken in *you*, and that lesson has been quietly running in the background of every job, every challenge, ever since. I notice you're speaking quite quickly, like there's a lot coming up at once, and even though you're describing something painful, there's also something that sounds almost like relief in finally saying it out loud. That connection you just made — between your dad's silence and the voice that tells you you don't belong in this role — that's not a small thing, and it deserves more than a quick acknowledgment.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech
